builder_plan.scenario: Tool errors or unavailable services cause your agent to abandon recoverable tasks.
builder_plan.change: Inject repeatable tool failures and change only the recovery policy.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current retry and fallback behavior under the same injected failures.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Recovered tasks, duplicate side effects, retries, time to recovery, and total cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Parsed, Plausible, Wrong: Output Format Controls Silent Errors in Small-Model Semantic Parsing
summary: It replaces terse symbolic target formats (e.g., s-expressions) in LoRA fine-tuning of sub-billion parsers with a lossless plain-words encoding of the same tree, at no extra infrastructure cost and with 4.1x fewer output tokens. The cost is a measured strict-refusal trade-off: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are rejected, and adopting the format requires retraining on re-encoded targets. It can fail because evidence comes from a single benchmark (PIZZA ordering), shortening alone never helped, so gains may not transfer to other domains, schemas, or models.
rationale: The encoding change is cheap and plausible for constrained setups, but it is validated on one ordering benchmark, so the reader should validate silent-error and refusal rates on their own workload before production adoption.
technique: Word-based output encoding for small-model semantic parsing

claims.statement: It replaces terse symbolic target formats (e.g., s-expressions) in LoRA fine-tuning of sub-billion parsers with a lossless plain-words encoding of the same tree, at no extra infrastructure cost and with 4.1x fewer output tokens. The cost is a measured strict-refusal trade-off: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are rejected, and adopting the format requires retraining on re-encoded targets. It can fail because evidence comes from a single benchmark (PIZZA ordering), shortening alone never helped, so gains may not transfer to other domains, schemas, or models.

A natural-word target encoding reaches 87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen3.5-0.8B while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens, and cuts the silent (well-formed but wrong) error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2.5-350M, with much of the gain in negation.
